title: What Not to Presume About Large-Scale Change
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article lays out four flawed assumptions leaders commonly make about organizational transformation and offers the more accurate counter-assumption for each. Leaders overestimate how much support already exists for a change, underestimate how long it will take to stick, assume people are more rational and persuadable than they actually are, and treat acceptance as a binary yes/no rather than a spectrum. The piece stresses that resistance often persists even after a change is implemented, sometimes surfacing as disengagement or open criticism, and that the education process has to continue long past when leaders assume it should end. It closes by framing successful transformation as a long, friction-filled process that demands persistence well beyond the initial rollout.
points: Leaders routinely overestimate how much genuine support already exists for a coming change.
Change takes far longer to take hold than leaders typically expect, no matter the organization's size.
People are not fully rational about change — for most, it feels stressful and unwanted, requiring persistence over persuasion.
Acceptance of change operates on a continuum, not as a simple accept/reject decision.
Even after implementation, some team members keep resisting, disengaging, or criticizing the change and its leaders.
quotes: Leaders commonly trust their own instincts when it comes to introducing and driving the change forward. They often make presumptions about the change process that severely limit their ability to successfully achieve their change goals.
Leaders typically believe there is more support for change than actually exists.
Unfortunately, for most people, change is stressful, uncomfortable, and unwanted. People prefer what they know and strongly resist accepting a new path.
Effective leaders understand it is persistence, and not just advocacy, that wins the day.
Creating change almost always takes more time, resources, persistence, and education than leaders expect it to.
